text.hook:
"Templates go in headers because .cpp files cannot hold them."
Wrong. The real rule is visibility at instantiation.

Swipe ➜ for the template rules interviewers probe, plus 6 myths.
text.body:
Inside:
1. Instantiation and why templates live in headers
2. The deduction table
3. Overload vs specialize
4. Disambiguators and CTAD
5. Folds and CRTP vs deducing this
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Deduction, specialization, dependent names, CTAD, folds and CRTP.

slides.title: A template is a recipe, not code

cards.label: Instantiation
cards.text: `max<int>` and `max<double>` are two separate functions in the binary.

cards.label: Headers
cards.text: The definition must be visible where it is instantiated. Else: "undefined reference".

cards.label: Control it
cards.text: `template class M<double>;` in one `.cpp`, `extern template` in the header.

slides.takeaway: Errors show up at instantiation, and every distinct argument set adds code (bloat).

slides.title: What is `T`?
slides.takeaway: By value makes a new copy, so top-level `const` goes. `T&` keeps everything the argument has.

slides.title: Overload, do not specialize functions

cards.label: Overload resolution
cards.text: Sees only primary templates and plain functions. Specializations are not candidates.

cards.label: Prefer
cards.text: Overloads, `if constexpr`, or a class template with partial specialization.

cards.label: No partial
cards.text: Function templates cannot be partially specialized. Class templates can.

slides.takeaway: A full specialization `f<int*>` is silently ignored if an overload `f(T*)` wins.

slides.title: Where correct-looking code fails
items: `typename T::value_type x;`: say it is a type
`std::array<int> a{1, 2}`: error, CTAD is all or nothing
slides.takeaway: A deduction guide fixes a CTAD surprise: `Wrapper(const char*) -> Wrapper<std::string>;`

slides.title: CRTP vs deducing this

cards.label: CRTP
cards.text: `struct D : Base<D>`. Base calls `static_cast<D&>(*this).step()`. No vptr.

cards.label: C++23
cards.text: `void run(this auto& self) { self.step(); }`. No template base, no cast (GCC 14+, Clang 18+).

slides.takeaway: CRTP removes the virtual call. Inlining is still the optimizer's decision.

items.truth: Only the non-dependent parts. Dependent code is checked at instantiation.
It is not a candidate. Only its primary template is.

items.myth: "Pass by value deduces `const int` from a `const int`."
"Function templates can be partially specialized, like classes."
"An empty fold works with any operator."
items.truth: Only `&&`, `||` and `,`. Others need an init value.

items.myth: "`typename` and `class` differ in a template parameter list."
items.truth: Identical there. `typename` also marks dependent types.

slides.hero:
A recipe, not code.
Overload, do not specialize.
Visible where instantiated.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
A two-line generic add.
Called with an int and a double.
"The int just converts to double." Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Ordinary functions convert arguments all the time. Templates play by a different rule.

slides.title: What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC: deduced conflicting types for parameter 'T' ('int' and 'double')
bullets: `T` is deduced from **each** argument separately: `int` from `10`, `double` from `20.5`.
All deductions of `T` must agree exactly. They do not.
Deduction never tries conversions, so the template is not viable: "no matching function".

slides.title: Fix `T` first, then convert
slides.code:
template <class A, class B>
auto add2(A a, B b) { return a + b; }

add<double>(10, 20.5);  // 30.5
add(10.0, 20.5);        // 30.5
add2(10, 20.5);         // 30.5
slides.tip: With an explicit `<double>` nothing is deduced, so `10` converts like in any normal call.
slides.takeaway: Conversions happen only after `T` is fixed.

text.hook:
Three vectors built from the same source.
C++17 CTAD deduces every element type.
They all hold 4 ints. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Braces vs parentheses is the whole puzzle.

slides.title: What does this print?

bullets: `a{src}`: for one argument of the same template, CTAD prefers the **copy** candidate: a `vector<int>` copy.
`b{...}`: braces make the `initializer_list` constructor win: two iterators.
`c(...)`: parentheses select the iterator-pair constructor and its deduction guide: 4 ints.
slides.wrong: "A: braces and parentheses do the same thing"

slides.title: Check the deduced type
slides.tip: Spelling out `<int>` turns CTAD off, so the braces can no longer pick iterators.
slides.takeaway: Iterator pairs: use parentheses or name the element type.

text.hook:
Cache inherits reset() from Storage.
Calling an inherited member is basic C++.
What could go wrong?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Without the templates this compiles fine. Add them and the compiler stops trusting the base.

slides.title: What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC: there are no arguments to 'reset' that depend on a template parameter
bullets: `Storage<T>` is a **dependent base**: unqualified lookup at definition time (phase 1) does not search it.
`reset()` has no dependent arguments, so it is looked up immediately. Nothing is found.

slides.title: Make the name dependent
slides.tip: Also fine: `Storage<T>::reset();` or `using Storage<T>::reset;` in the class.
slides.takeaway: Members of a dependent base need `this->` or qualification.

text.hook:
"A plain function always beats a template."
Two plain overloads, one template, three calls.
The last one is a short.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The first two calls are warm-up. The third is the interview question.

slides.title: What does this print?

slides.verdict_sub: The non-template preference is only a tie-breaker
bullets: `handle(1)`: `handle(int)` and `handle<int>` are both exact. Tie: the non-template wins.
`handle(1L)`: same tie with `long`: the non-template wins.
`handle(s)`: `handle<short>` is **exact**. `handle(int)` needs a promotion, `handle(long)` a conversion.
The better match is decided before "prefer non-template" is ever asked.
slides.wrong: "A: short promotes to int, plain function wins"

slides.title: Remove the template
bullets: Order: exact match, then promotion, then conversion.
Only on a tie: non-template beats template.
Still tied: the more specialized template wins.
slides.takeaway: "Prefer the non-template" is a tie-breaker, not a rule.
